title: Cherry-pick, revert, and moving a fix deliberately
outcome: Move a small fix between release lines and distinguish patch replay from history preservation.
benefits: Small fixes can move without unrelated features.
drawbacks: Dependencies and merge semantics can make a small patch nontrivial.
version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability
cue: Move the patch. Check its assumptions.

trace.title: Inspect fix
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Cherry-pick applies a commit’s change onto the current base and usually creates a new commit. It does not bring every dependency of that change automatically.

A patch that applies cleanly can still call a helper absent on the release branch.

Revert creates a new corrective commit. It is often easier for collaborators than rewriting a published branch.

Reverting a merge requires choosing the intended mainline parent and understanding future merge consequences; do not guess from parent numbers.

Before any history operation, inspect the graph, outgoing patch, and current work. Use a disposable worktree for a release rehearsal.

Record which release line received the fix and how it was tested there.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Fix on main → inspect dependencies → replay onto release branch → resolve intent → test release configuration → review. The new commit ID can differ even when the patch is similar.

For a revert, test the resulting behavior with later changes present. A reverse patch is not a reversal of every external effect or migration.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
A clean cherry-pick can be behaviorally incomplete. Reverting a migration commit does not reconstruct deleted data.

Shared branch rewrites need coordination.
